newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin crowns Kremlin return but questions remain.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin crowns Kremlin return but questions remain.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's fit and vigorous appearance in his state of the nation speech on Thursday signalled he is back at the helm in Russia, silencing the critics who said he would never return from illness.

But the 66-year-old leader's revival has still failed to answer some questions -- is he capable of restoring the faded charisma which helped him guide Russia from communism to democracy and how firm is his grip on power after so long on the sidelines?
"No doubt Yeltsin is coming back as a national leader," one government official, who asked not to be named, said after hearing the president's speech.
"But he has lost much of his public appeal and he now faces strong political groups which have emerged on the Russian scene."
Yeltsin, who has been seen in public only rarely since his re-election last July because of health problems, has staged his public comeback with due sabre-rattling.

Last week he summoned Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and criticised him for letting an economic and social crisis get out of hand. Then he scolded his chief prosecutor for mishandling the fight against crime.

His 25-minute speech to parliament was full of criticism of the government, which is expected to be dramatically reshuffled, and populilst vows to protect common people from bureaucracy, which had gone "fat".

"I saw a tough Yeltsin, exactly the man we adored in 1987," Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov said of Yeltsin's speech with a touch of nostalgia for when the silver-haired rebel launched his crusade against communism.

Yeltsin also used his speech indirectly to hit back at critics who say the president's long absences from work, first with heart problems and then with pneumonia, had played a nasty trick on him by showing he was not needed.
Despite his absence, they say, Russia's political system has remained relatively stable.

Yeltsin disagrees. "The executive power proved to be incapable of working without the president's whip," he said defiantly. "We must restore order, first of all in the government, and I shall do this."

Yeltsin was in effect resorting to two things that have helped Russian leaders for centuries -- people's longing for order and their traditional belief that the leader's good intentions are distorted by his plotting entourage.

He painted a picture of decay in Russia, with people not getting paid, the economy strangled by non-payments and the bureaucracy corroded by corruption, in an effort to stress the problems that have piled up without him.
In effect, he shifted the blame on to others and named his medicine -- strict order based on the law.

"At the end of March people in many cities intend to take part in protest actions and these protests are to a large extent justified," Yeltsin said. "This is a warning signal, a sign that the patience of the people is reaching its limits."
His communist opponents, who say they represent a large section of society, appeared unimpressed. They made clear they believed Yeltsin was still to blame.

"It's nice to hear from the president that things are bad. But who is to blame for the situation when the economy is falling apart and people do not get their pay," communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said.
Independent political commentators have suggested Yeltsin's physical comeback does not necessarily mean he can take complete power again.
They say powerful political groups which ruled the country in his absence, personified by a few top officials, will not easily give up the positions they have gained.

Most speculation centres on Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, 41, who has a reputation of the "Kremlin kingmaker", and Chernomyrdin, 58, often seen as a natural Kremlin choice for the next president.
Both officials played a prominent role in Yeltsin's re-election last summer and continually vow loyalty to him.
Russian newspapers have said that large financial groups are also behind the leading political players and will also defend their positions.
"Yeltsin remains a crucial stabilising part of the Russian political mechanism," the government official said.
"But the difference is that there are other parts in the mechanism now which he has to take into account."
